text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Initial evaluation and safety: blood count, iron studies and metabolic panel; Glasgow-Blatchford score; stop ibuprofen and all NSAIDs and use acetaminophen; urgent upper endoscopy within three days; no acid-suppressing medicine or antibiotic before the biopsies unless bleeding recurs; call 119 or go to the emergency department at once for black or bloody stools, vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, fainting, or severe pain
  • Urgent gastroenterology consultation for upper endoscopy with biopsy within three days, to find the cause of the bleeding, exclude gastric cancer, test for Helicobacter pylori, and advise on treatment
  • Iron-deficiency anemia: oral iron once the source is found at endoscopy; blood count about four weeks after starting iron and then every three months for a year; continue iron about three months after the hemoglobin is normal and until ferritin is replete; colonoscopy if the anemia does not correct once the ulcer has healed
  • Stress and sleep: PHQ-9 and GAD-7 at intake and at the end of the episode; regular meals, a fixed bedtime, and writing hours that leave the evening free; counselling if scores rise
  • Gastric ulcer and Helicobacter pylori: vonoprazan 20 mg each morning for eight weeks; eradication chosen by the biopsy resistance result (vonoprazan 20 mg twice daily with amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 14 days for a clarithromycin-resistant strain); 13C urea breath test at least four weeks after the antibiotics and two weeks after vonoprazan; repeat endoscopy with biopsy of the scar at about ten weeks
  • Gastric cancer surveillance after eradication: upper endoscopy yearly because of moderate atrophy with intestinal metaplasia in the antrum (OLGA stage II), lifelong; no smoking, little alcohol and less salt
  • Acute low back strain: stay active, superficial heat, gentle stretching, and acetaminophen up to 3 g a day for a few days; no ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin or other NSAID, including topical or combination cold remedies, while the ulcer heals and preferably for good; finish the eradication course; return for leg weakness, numbness in the saddle area, loss of bladder or bowel control, fever, or pain that is not easing in four weeks
  • Prediabetes: walking at least 150 minutes a week, regular meals with less refined rice and sweets, and weight kept steady; repeat A1c in three months once iron is replete, then yearly

resource.title: Natsume Sōseki synthetic care plan
resource.description: Recognize a bleeding peptic ulcer in a 43-year-old novelist in Tokyo with epigastric pain, black stools and iron-deficiency anemia, and care for it as Japanese and international guidance advise: a Glasgow-Blatchford score and clear instructions on when to call 119; stopping NSAIDs; urgent upper endoscopy with biopsy of the ulcer margin to exclude gastric cancer, which is common in Japan, and mapping biopsies for Helicobacter pylori and atrophy; acid suppression with vonoprazan; H. pylori eradication chosen by local resistance and the patient's own susceptibility result (vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy for a clarithromycin-resistant strain, because bismuth quadruple therapy is not available for this use in Japan); confirmation of eradication by urea breath test off acid suppression; repeat endoscopy to confirm healing of a gastric ulcer; oral iron with monitoring of the blood count (CMID anemia monograph); advice on alcohol and smoking; stress and depression screening; and endoscopic surveillance for gastric cancer after eradication because of atrophy and intestinal metaplasia. The modern episode is a teaching case, not a claim about the cause of his real illness.
